(CNN) -- A federal judge has stayed what would be the nation's first military execution since 1961, saying the U.S. soldier -- who was convicted of rape and murder two decades ago -- should have more time to pursue a federal appeal. Pvt. Ronald Gray has been on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, since 1988. A court-martial panel sitting at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, unanimously convicted him of committing two murders and other crimes in the Fayetteville, North Carolina, area and sentenced him to death. Last month, the Army said Gray was scheduled to be executed by lethal injection December 10 at the Federal Correctional Complex in Terre Haute, Indiana. But in an order issued November 26, U.S. District Judge Richard Rogers of Kansas said that a stay is necessary so Gray can pursue his federal appeal. Rogers ruled on a motion filed by Gray's attorneys, who asked for time to challenge the legality of his convictions and sentence. Government attorneys have asked Rogers to reconsider his decision, saying that Gray seeks a stay "apparently based on the premise that at some point he will identify a new legal issue or discover new evidence" upon which to appeal and that Gray "continues to delay unnecessarily." Gray has had ample time to appeal, the Justice Department attorneys said. In a response filed Tuesday, Gray's defense attorneys point out that the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in March 2001, and "since then, it has taken the Department of the Army, the Department of Defense, the Department of Justice and the Office of the President over seven years to approve as final Private Gray's sentence of death. The significant constitutional issues presented on the face of Private Gray's case ... have obviously troubled the decision-makers, as evidenced by the years they had his case under advisement." President Bush approved Gray's death sentence in July, making it final, defense attorneys write in the filing. Inmates sentenced to death in state and federal courts are given a year to file federal appeals after their death sentence becomes final, they claim, and members of the military under death sentences should receive the same consideration. "Private Gray is seeking federal habeas court review for the first time and he has not delayed commencing this action," defense attorney Thomas Bath wrote. "In fact, until the president approved his death sentence, there was no action available." Gray was convicted of raping and killing a female Army private and a civilian near his post at Fort Bragg. He also was convicted of the rape and attempted murder of another fellow soldier in her barracks at the post. Military and civilian courts both found Gray responsible for the crimes, which were committed between April 1986 and January 1987. Gray pleaded guilty to two murders and five rapes in a civilian court and was sentenced to three consecutive and five concurrent life terms. The general court-martial at Fort Bragg then tried him and in April 1988 convicted him of two murders, an attempted murder and three rapes. Bush's July action, the Army said in a statement at the time, followed "completion of a full appellate process, which upheld the conviction and sentence to death." Members of the U.S. military have been executed throughout history, but just 10 have been executed with presidential approval since 1951 under the Uniform Code of Military justice, the military's modern-day legal system. The Army has also sought Bush's authorization to execute another condemned soldier, Pvt. Dwight Loving, who was convicted of killing and robbing two cab drivers in 1988. The last U.S. military execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged for raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old Austrian girl. Bennett was sentenced in 1955. The U.S. military hasn't actively pursued an execution for a military prisoner since President Kennedy commuted a death sentence in 1962. Nine men are currently on military death row. CNN's Mike Mount contributed to this report.

**Delayed Execution of Ronald Gray Would Be First U.S. Military Execution Since 1961**

**By [News Desk]**

The planned execution of former Army Pvt. Ronald A. Gray — the first proposed execution by the U.S. military in more than six decades — has been delayed amid continuing legal challenges over his conviction, sentence and access to federal court review.

Gray, a former soldier stationed at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, was sentenced to death by a military court in 1988 for a series of rapes and murders committed in the 1980s. His case has long stood as one of the most closely watched military capital prosecutions in modern U.S. history because no service member has been executed by the military since 1961.

The last military execution was that of Army Pvt. John A. Bennett, who was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after being convicted of rape and attempted murder. Since then, military death sentences have been rare, and none has been carried out.

Gray’s execution, which had been planned to take place by lethal injection at the federal execution chamber in Terre Haute, Indiana, was postponed after defense attorneys pursued further court review. The delay continues a decades-long legal battle over whether Gray’s death sentence should be carried out.

## The Crimes and Conviction

Ronald Gray was convicted by a military court-martial of multiple offenses, including murder, rape, attempted murder and robbery. The victims included civilian women near Fort Bragg, where Gray was assigned.

Military prosecutors described Gray’s crimes as exceptionally brutal and argued during trial and post-trial proceedings that the evidence of guilt was overwhelming. Gray also faced civilian convictions in North Carolina related to some of the same crime spree.

His military death sentence was reviewed through the military justice system, including the Army Court of Military Review and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces. Under military law, a death sentence cannot be carried out unless it is approved by the president. President George W. Bush approved Gray’s execution in 2008, making him the first president in decades to authorize a military execution.

## Prosecutors: “A Lawful Sentence After Exhaustive Review”

Government attorneys have argued that Gray received all process required under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Constitution.

Prosecutors contend that Gray’s case has been reviewed repeatedly for decades by military and civilian courts, and that the sentence was lawfully imposed by a court-martial. They have emphasized the severity of the crimes and the number of victims, arguing that the death penalty was justified by the facts of the case.

In filings and prior arguments, government lawyers have maintained that Gray’s claims were either already considered and rejected or were filed too late. They have also argued that federal courts should give significant deference to the military justice system, which has its own appellate structure and procedures.

The government’s position has generally rested on several points:

- **Finality of judgment:** Prosecutors say Gray has had decades of appeals and collateral review, and that the legal process should eventually come to an end.
- **Validity of the military trial:** They argue the court-martial was properly conducted and that Gray was represented by counsel.
- **Presidential approval:** Because the president approved the sentence, prosecutors say the military met the special statutory requirement for carrying out a death sentence.
- **Deference to military courts:** The government argues civilian courts should not relitigate issues fully considered by military tribunals unless there is a clear constitutional defect.

Prosecutors have also pointed to the victims and their families, arguing that the extended delay has denied them closure.

## Defense: Constitutional Questions Remain

Defense attorneys have argued that Gray’s execution should not proceed until federal courts fully examine constitutional challenges to his conviction and sentence.

They have raised concerns about whether Gray received effective assistance of counsel, whether the military death-penalty process was applied fairly, and whether his rights were adequately protected during the investigation, trial and sentencing phases. Defense lawyers have also argued that the extraordinary length of time between sentencing and execution underscores the need for careful judicial scrutiny.

In military capital cases, defense attorneys often challenge both the trial proceedings and the structure of the military death penalty itself. Gray’s lawyers have sought habeas corpus review in federal court, arguing that even though the military courts reviewed the case, civilian courts retain authority to examine whether the Constitution was violated.

Key defense arguments have included:

- **Right to meaningful federal review:** Defense attorneys say a military death sentence should be subject to searching review by Article III courts before an execution occurs.
- **Ineffective assistance claims:** They have argued that Gray’s legal representation at various stages failed to adequately investigate or present mitigating evidence.
- **Due process concerns:** The defense has questioned aspects of the military justice process and whether Gray’s constitutional rights were fully protected.
- **Eighth Amendment issues:** Defense attorneys have argued that capital punishment must meet heightened reliability standards, especially in a system that has not carried out an execution in generations.

The defense has also stressed the unusual nature of the case: because the military has not executed anyone since 1961, Gray’s execution would set a historic precedent and should not proceed while unresolved legal claims remain.

## A Rare Military Death Penalty Case

The military death penalty exists under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, but it is used infrequently. Death sentences must pass through automatic military appellate review and then receive presidential approval. Even after that, prisoners may seek review in federal civilian courts.

Military executions are now carried out by lethal injection, typically at the federal facility in Terre Haute. Historically, military executions were conducted by hanging or firing squad.

Gray’s case is significant not only because of the severity of the crimes, but because it tests the modern military capital punishment system — a system that has been authorized on paper but dormant in practice for more than half a century.

## Victims’ Families and Broader Impact

For families of Gray’s victims, the delay has prolonged a case that began in the 1980s. Supporters of the execution argue that Gray’s guilt has long been established and that the punishment was affirmed through extensive review.

Opponents of the execution, including some death-penalty critics, argue that the delay illustrates deeper problems with capital punishment, especially within a military legal system that operates differently from civilian courts.

Legal observers say the case raises major questions about the relationship between military justice and federal judicial oversight. While courts traditionally defer to military tribunals, death penalty cases receive heightened scrutiny because of the irreversible nature of execution.

## What Comes Next

Gray’s execution remains delayed while legal proceedings continue. Any final execution date would require the government to clear remaining judicial obstacles and comply with military and federal execution protocols.

If carried out, Gray’s execution would mark the first time the U.S. military has put a service member to death since the Kennedy administration. Until then, his case remains a landmark test of military capital punishment, federal habeas review and the long reach of justice in one of the military’s most notorious criminal cases.

The stay halted what would have been the U.S. military’s first execution since 1961. Gray, held at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, was facing execution by lethal injection after Bush approved the sentence in 2008, a step required before a military death sentence can be carried out.

Laura Lee Vickery-Clay and civilian Kimberly Ann Ruggles, as well as rape, attempted murder and other assaults. The Supreme Court declined to disturb the conviction and sentence.

After the execution date was set, Gray’s attorneys sought federal habeas review, arguing that he was entitled to challenge the legality of his conviction and death sentence in civilian court. The federal court stay allows that litigation to proceed.

The government opposed delaying the execution, arguing that Gray had received extensive review during more than two decades of military and civilian proceedings and that the judgment should be carried out. Prosecutors and military officials have maintained that Gray’s conviction and sentence were lawful and final.

Gray’s case stands out in the modern military death penalty system. Although courts-martial may impose death for certain aggravated offenses, executions are exceedingly rare.
